newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Belgian OLOs in quiet patch, no storm brewing.
newsitem.headline: Belgian OLOs in quiet patch, no storm brewing.

text.p: Belgian government bonds (OLOs) were quietly firmer on Monday and dealers expected the "roaring silence" to continue for the rest of this holiday-thinned week.

The release of German March output data fell on deaf ears as did talk of a fall in German unemployment DE-ECI. Official figures are due on Tuesday. No major U.S. numbers are due until next week, starving the market of factors and direction.

This left players with only the French election campaign and opinion polls to focus on FR-POL. Analysts said nervousness about the outcome of the vote and its impact on the prospects for EMU could flare up again in the three weeks ahead.
"Should France end up with a socialist government, there would be durable doubts about the future of EMU," an analyst said. This would hit OLOs' convergence with German Bunds.
OLOs were firmer on Monday, continuing Friday's advance on benign U.S. data, but volumes were slim and a pick-up in investor appetite was unlikely this week, dealers said.

Many blamed the Spring bank holiday closure of London markets today, an absence of major U.S. data this week and market holidays in Belgium on Thursday and Friday. The various factors meant OLOs would be range-bound this week, dealers said.
"The market will take a breather," said an analyst.

The 10-year OLO/Bund spread widened to 11 basis points at 1445 GMT from 10 on Friday as some of the pressure on French OATs from the election worries wafted over to the Belgian market MEUR. But dealers said there was no reason to expect that the current 10-15 bp range would be cracked.
One analyst said that after the benchmark OLO BE296= gained over a full point in the past week it was looking overbought. "A downward correction in the coming days cannot be excluded."
But another said there was little downward pressure with institutionals expected to continue to hug the sidelines.

There was no noticeable fallout from news that Belgian tax authorities were investigating a confidential report that foreign leaders, political parties, sects and private persons were laundering cash through bank accounts in Luxembourg.

In the longer term there might be an effect of such news, an analyst said, with cash being repatriated. But at the moment it remained "fiscally interesting" to have money in bank accounts in Luxembourg where banking secrecy is strictly observed.

Money laundering is not a crime in the Grand Duchy, while it is in Belgium. Also there is no withholding tax on interest earned. -- Nieck Ammerlaan, Brussels Newsroom +32 2 287 6816, Fax +32 2 230 7710
